newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU ministers to meet on EMU, cheered by Kohl.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers to meet on EMU, cheered by Kohl.

text.p: EU finance ministers, buoyed by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's decision to seek re-election, headed on Friday for a two-day meeting in the Netherlands hoping to regain the high ground over euro-doubters.

Following a welter of speculation about a delay in the planned 1999 start-date for economic and monetary union (EMU), the 15 ministers will be cheered by Thursday's announcement that Kohl, the key figure behind the single currency, is to stand for a fifth term of office in next year's elections.
Kohl's decision gave a shot in the arm to the pro-EMU camp, which appears to have been out-shouted in recent weeks by those who doubt the euro project can start on schedule.
German participation in the first wave of EMU is seen as critical to the venture's success.

But, with the German jobless total at a 64-year high, the last time more than 4.5 million were out of work being when Hitler rose to power, and Bonn risking worker unrest in a determined bid to cut spending to meet EMU criteria, many have begun to doubt the single currency can start on time.
Analysts said markets were looking at the Noordwijk meeting with a more upbeat view on the viability of the EMU project.
"There are a couple of things going on in the background which are helping to shore up confidence," said Andrew Bevan, senior bond economist at Goldman Sachs in London.
One factor was the renewed sense of commitment shown by Kohl with his announcement he would run again in 1998.

The other, Bevan said, was the recent set of unexpectedly strong economic data in Germany. It needs an economic pickup to improve the ratio between its fiscal deficit and gross domestic product (GDP) -- one of the key targets that EU nations must meet to qualify for EMU.

Converging on the Dutch seaside town of Noordwijk, ministers and central bankers will address the problems of sluggish European growth, rising unemployment and last-ditch efforts of some members to meet the conditions for joining the single currency.
Those wanting to take part in EMU, scheduled to start in January 1999, must bring their 1997 budget deficits close to three percent of GDP under the targets set by the Maastricht Treaty.

The ministers, who are expected to reaffirm a commitment to EMU's 1999 launch date, will have welcomed Thursday's news of a recovery in German industrial output which rebounded in February to a 1.9 percent rise after January's 1.5 percent fall.
"There is reason for some optimism as the (output) numbers now present a slightly stronger picture for economic growth," one German economist said on Thursday.
Ministers will try on Saturday to set a date next year for choosing which states join EMU from the start. The odds favour late April 1998.

This would allow France to put its parliamentary election behind it. It would also give time to consider reports, due next February, from the European Commission and the European Monetary Institute (EMI) on the degree of economic convergence within the 15-nation bloc based on reliable economic data for 1997.

European Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy reiterated in a French newspaper interview on Friday that the Maastricht Treaty did not allow for any delay in launching EMU, only for it to be brought forward, in the right conditions.
Ministers in Noordwijk will also review progress on some of EMU's technical aspects, relating mainly to putting a stability and growth pact into a legal context.
The pact, which seeks to penalise governments running excessive budget deficits -- above three percent of GDP -- inside EMU, was agreed last December.
They will also take stock of negotiations on a revamped Exchange Rate Mechanism designed to link countries outside EMU to the euro.
